title: Computational reproducibility of Jupyter notebooks from biomedical publications

cost.compute_notes: arXiv PDF 2.07 MB read as pdftotext -layout (1,927 lines). Analysis repo shallow-cloned (50 MB, commit 138cc62); PMC3 and PMC4 notebooks read cell by cell INCLUDING their stored outputs, which is where the decay table and the combining logic live. Zenodo archive 96.7 MB downloaded, from which the 371 MB db.sqlite was extracted, queried with stdlib sqlite3, and DELETED -- the two fetch commands are in reanalysis/cluster_and_age.py. Three reanalysis scripts, stdlib only, together under 20 s on CPU.

claims.statement: Of 27,271 Jupyter notebooks from 2,660 GitHub repositories associated with 3,467 PubMed Central publications, 1,203 ran through without any errors, of which 879 produced results identical to those recorded in the original notebook.
claims.scope: 2023 re-run. Only Python notebooks whose dependencies were declared in a standard requirements file were attempted (15,817); only those whose declared dependencies all installed were executed (10,388). Executed in conda environments, per-notebook timeout 300 s.

our_assessment.why: The 2021 funnel reproduces to the file from the shipped SQLite database (4,169 attempted / 396 finished / 245 identical / 151 different, against the paper's printed 4,169 / 396 / 245 / 151). Accepted without qualification, and this study is the best-instrumented in this area: it prints EVERY stage of the funnel rather than one ratio, so a reader can choose the denominator instead of inheriting one. The multiple values recorded above are not a criticism of the paper -- they are the paper's own ladder, written down so that a future citation cannot lose which rung it came from.

claims.statement: Notebooks from newer repositories do not generally perform better than older ones -- the relationship between recency and exceptions is 'a bit more complex'.
claims.scope: The paper's Figure 27 and the shipped notebook analyses/PMC4.DecayRate.ipynb, titled 'Decay Rate: Replication Success over Repository Age'. Repository age is 2023 minus the GitHub repository creation year.

quantities.baseline: 2023 run, repositories created in 2013 (age 10) -- the oldest cohort surviving the authors' filter

quantities.name: artifact_execution_success_rate
quantities.baseline: 2021 run, repositories created in 2013 -- SAME cohort, same pipeline, two years earlier

quantities.name: cohort_rate_ratio_between_two_runs_of_one_pipeline
quantities.baseline: 2013 cohort: 48.9% in the 2023 run over 4.7% in the 2021 run

our_assessment.why: The understatement hides a large effect and the effect changes sign between the study's own two runs. In the 2023 table the association is strongly POSITIVE (older reproduces better; trend z = +11.7, OR 1.166/year, surviving a clustering correction all the way to ICC = 1 and a synthetic clustered null whose 95th percentile |z| is 2.96). In the 2021 database it is NEGATIVE (z = -4.40 at notebook level, -1.87 at repository level). Cohort by cohort the rate ratio between runs reaches 10.5x on a cohort of nearly identical size. The reason is structural and is not anyone's error: the pipeline conditions on the declared dependencies INSTALLING before a notebook is executed, and failing to install is decay's primary mechanism -- so decay removes its own victims upstream of the outcome, and what remains in the old cohorts is survivors. An age effect measured under survivor conditioning carries the sign of the survival filter. The claim has no truth value in this design. NOTE ALSO: the authors' notebook filters to cohorts with more than 10 successes, which deletes 2010-2012, whose pooled rate (14/60 = 23.3%, recovered by subtraction) is roughly twice the corpus rate -- the filter removes evidence FOR the association the figure shows.

our_assessment.why: Not a claim the paper makes explicitly, which is the problem: it is an unstated design assumption underneath every percentage in the Results. Every notebook in a repository shares one conda environment, one set of data paths and one author, and the measured ICC is 0.435. 77.2% of repositories contributing three or more executions had a completely homogeneous outcome -- a repository is close to one Bernoulli trial. The effective n is about a third of the printed one, and the finer the slice (per journal, per field, per year) the more likely it reports a single repository. All 396 successes of the 2021 run come from 130 repositories, with the top 20 supplying 57%. This does not touch the headline rate, which is a simple proportion; it undermines every comparison built on top of it.

claims.statement: The large majority of notebooks could not be executed automatically, mostly due to issues with the documentation of dependencies -- so better dependency documentation is the key intervention.
claims.scope: Key Points and Conclusions; the same recommendation is the first in Trisovic et al. 2022 and a fixture of the reproducibility-guidance literature.

quantities.baseline: 2021 run; logistic regression adjusted for log dependency count, licence and log stars; SE 0.644, 22 events

our_assessment.why: The first half is true and reproduces; the recommendation attached to it has never been tested, and this is the dataset that can test it because it ships the verbatim CONTENT of every requirements file next to the outcome. Restricting to the 191 repositories that declared requirements -- repositories with none are not a control, they receive a large default conda environment -- the point estimate runs AGAINST the recommendation at every stratum: OR 0.435 unadjusted (Fisher p = 0.29), adjusted log-odds -0.392 (z = -0.61), and all six pre-specified strata by licence / releases / stars negative (z between -0.99 and -2.08). With 22 events this cannot establish that pinning HURTS and I do not claim it does. It does establish that the field's most repeated recommendation is untested and that the only data able to test it fail to support it. The mechanism is visible at the install stage (23.4% vs 40.4%, z = -1.77) and is not mysterious: 'numpy==1.16.4' instructs a 2023 toolchain to build a 2019 wheel. A pin is a PROVENANCE record and a PORTABILITY liability, and the guidance literature conflates the two. What preserves executability is a built environment, not a list of version numbers.

claims.statement: The low degree of reproducibility found here agrees with similarly low levels found in earlier domain-generic studies, for Python and for R.
claims.scope: Discussion, citing Pimentel et al. 2019 and Trisovic et al. 2022 among others.

quantities.name: artifact_execution_success_rate
quantities.baseline: Pimentel et al. 2019, GitHub-wide Python notebooks with unambiguous execution order; 208,323 successes

quantities.name: artifact_reproduction_identical_output_rate
quantities.baseline: Pimentel et al. 2019, notebooks that ran AND produced the same results

quantities.name: artifact_build_success_rate
quantities.baseline: Collberg & Proebsting TR 14-04 (Feb 2015), 'weak repeatability A': code obtained and built within 30 minutes, of ACM papers backed by code

quantities.name: artifact_build_success_rate
quantities.baseline: Collberg & Proebsting, 'weak repeatability C': built by us, or the author states it would build with reasonable effort

our_assessment.why: The low rates do agree in the sense that all of them are low. They do not agree numerically, and the appearance that they do is partly manufactured by quoting across incommensurable funnels. Documented instance: Pimentel et al. write that their 24.11% 'is close to the reproducibility rate of 24.9% that Collberg et al. achieved'; the Collberg TR I read reports 32.3% / 48.3% / 54.0% of 402 code-backed papers, and 24.9% comes from the superseded 2014 version they cite. The two events are also not the same event -- a C/C++ project BUILDING versus a notebook RUNNING TO COMPLETION -- on populations that share nothing. Every one of these numbers is a proportion whose denominator was chosen partway down a funnel, and the choices differ between studies. See maria2026-executability-denominators for the pooled version.

datasheet.motivation: Full record of the 2021 run of the reproducibility pipeline.
datasheet.composition: SQLite, 371 MB. One row per execution attempt in `executions` (notebook_id, repository_id, reason, msg, diff, processed bitfield, duration). Outcome is encoded in `processed`: finished = (processed & 44) == 32; identical output = additionally (processed & 16). `repository_data` carries GitHub metadata including created_at, stars, releases, licence. `requirement_files` carries the verbatim content of every setup.py / requirements.txt / Pipfile.
datasheet.collection: Mined PubMed Central full text for GitHub links, cloned, built conda environments from declared requirements, executed notebooks with a 300 s per-notebook timeout, diffed outputs with nbdime.
datasheet.preprocessing: None in the archive; the filtering happens in the analysis notebooks.
datasheet.caveats: THIS IS THE 2021 RUN, not the 2023 run the published paper's headline numbers describe (1,419 articles / 2,177 repos / 9,625 notebooks here, against 3,467 / 2,660 / 27,271 there). I did not locate a Zenodo record for the 2023 database. Second caveat: rows are notebooks and notebooks are strongly clustered in repositories (ICC 0.435); anything computed per notebook needs a design-effect correction. Third: `reason` is NULL for successes, so a naive count of non-null reasons is not a failure count.

checked.how: transcribed by hand from the notebook's stored dataframe; the three cohorts the authors' >10-successes filter deletes were recovered by subtraction (10389 total executions - 10329 in the kept cohorts = 60; 1203 total successes - 1189 kept = 14) and the recovery reconciles exactly on the success side
checked.result: 11 cohorts, 1203 successes in 10389 executions. This is the 2023 run's decay table and it exists NOWHERE in the paper except as an unlabelled figure -- the numbers are only obtainable by reading the shipped notebook's output. Provenance and the subtraction are documented inside the CSV header.

checked.how: cd reanalysis && python age_trend.py > age_trend.log && python cluster_and_age.py > cluster_and_age.log
checked.result: age_trend.py: trend tests on the 2023 cohort table with the deleted cohorts restored, a clustering sensitivity sweep over ICC 0 to 1, and a synthetic clustered null in which the naive test fires 21% of the time against a nominal 5%. cluster_and_age.py: reproduces the 2021 funnel from the database, measures ICC and the design effect, redoes the age trend at both notebook and repository level, and puts the two runs side by side cohort for cohort.

Parses requirement_files.content into pinning classes, then compares repository-level execution outcomes across them, with a Fisher exact test, a stdlib Newton-Raphson logistic regression adjusted for dependency count / licence / stars, and stratification on three maintenance proxies. 191 repositories, 22 events -- underpowered and reported as such.

relations.why: Same estimand (does deposited research code re-execute in a clean environment), different language, different repository, and rates that are low in both. The agreement is qualitative only -- see c5 and maria2026-executability-denominators for why the numerical agreement across this literature is largely an artifact of incommensurable funnels.

Not a correction of Trisovic's arithmetic but of its practice, and it is the constructive half of that record. Trisovic chooses a denominator silently inside a notebook and prints one ratio; Samuel & Mietchen print every stage of the funnel. Given the same underlying problem, the second design lets a reader pick the rung and the first does not.
relations.asymmetric_note: The reciprocal is NOT that trisovic2022 corrects anything here. It runs the other way only.

relations.why: Jo et al.: a monoculture statistic is a discrepancy from a null the analyst chooses. Here: a reproducibility rate is a proportion whose denominator the analyst chooses partway down a funnel. The difference from the trisovic2022 instance of this edge is that here the choice is PRINTED -- which protects the headline and, as c2 shows, does not protect the sub-analyses built on the conditioned subset.

Two runs of ONE pipeline by ONE team two years apart give opposite signs for the age-reproducibility association (z = -4.40 then z = +11.7). That is many-analysts dispersion with n = 1 analyst: when an estimand is conditioned on an unstable upstream filter, no analyst degrees of freedom are needed to produce the dispersion. Sharpens the Breznau reading rather than contradicting it.

Reciprocal, on concentration. 77% of repositories here with three or more notebooks had a homogeneous outcome and 130 repositories produced all 396 successes; there, 63% of articles had zero major errors and the top 10 hold 95% of them. Two corpora, two units, same shape: a value-level or file-level rate is not a per-paper hazard.

open_questions: Redo the pinning test (c4) on the 2023 corpus, where n is about 3x larger. 22 events is not enough to say anything and the 2023 run might reach the point where it is.
Name the one or two repositories driving the 2013 cohort's 10.5x jump between runs. That would settle whether the entire 'old code reproduces better' pattern is a single artifact.

Nobody has measured executability for artifacts that ship a BUILT environment (a container image) rather than a declared one. If Trisovic's recommendation #4 is right, that rate should be far above 12%, and it is the only version of this measurement that would change anyone's behaviour.

The paper reports exception rates by journal ranging above 50% and below 20%. Given ICC 0.435 and 130 repositories producing all successes, most of those are one-repository differences. Recomputing them at repository level is cheap and would probably delete a table.

The FAIR Jupyter knowledge graph (arXiv 2404.12935, same authors) is this dataset as RDF with a SPARQL endpoint. Whether querying it is genuinely cheaper than sqlite3 over the dump is an open and directly testable question about whether semantic publishing pays for itself -- and it is a knowledge-management question, not a biomedical one.
